en: Majjhima Nikāya 140,
Dhātuvibhaṅgasutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion, while wandering on tour among the Magadhans, the Blessed One arrived at Rājagaha;
he approached the potter Bhaggava and, having approached him, said this to the potter Bhaggava:
"If it is not troublesome for you, Bhaggava, we would stay one night in your workshop."
“It is not troublesome for me, venerable sir.
There is a wanderer who has already arrived here to take up residence.
If he permits it, then stay as you please, venerable sir.”
Now at that time, a clansman named Pukkusāti had gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, dedicated to the Blessed One.
He was the first to take up residence in that potter’s workshop.
Then the Blessed One approached the Venerable Pukkusāti and, having approached, said this to him:
“If it is not troublesome for you, monk, let us stay one night in the workshop.
“The potter’s workshop is spacious, friend;
may the venerable one stay there as he pleases.”
Then the Blessed One entered the potter’s workshop, prepared a grass mat at one side, and sat down cross-legged with his body erect, having established mindfulness before him.
Then the Blessed One spent most of the night in a sitting posture.
The Venerable Pukkusāti also spent most of the night in a sitting posture.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"This clansman conducts himself in a pleasing manner.
What if I were to question him?"
Then the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Pukkusāti:
“Bhikkhu, for whose sake have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Or whose Dhamma do you approve of?
“There is, friend, a recluse named Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan clan.”
Now, this excellent report concerning the Blessed One Gotama has spread abroad:

“Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
It is with reference to that Blessed One that I have gone forth.
“And that Blessed One is my teacher.
And I delight in the Dhamma of that Blessed One.
“But where, monk, does that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwell at present?”
“There is, friends, in the northern countries a city named Sāvatthī.
There the Blessed One is currently residing; he is the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
“But, bhikkhu, have you ever seen that Blessed One before?”
"And having seen him, would you recognize him?
"I have never before seen that Blessed One, friend;
even if I had seen him, I would not recognize him."
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“This clansman has gone forth specifically for my sake;
what if I were to teach him the Dhamma?”
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Pukkusāti:
"Bhikkhu, I shall teach you the Dhamma.
Listen to it and attend closely; I will speak."
“Yes, friend,” the Venerable Pukkusāti replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhu, this person consists of six elements, has six bases for contact, eighteen mental explorations, and four foundations.
‘Wherein, when one stands firm, the currents of conceiving do not flow; and when the currents of conceiving do not flow, the sage is said to be at peace.
One should not neglect wisdom, one should guard truth, one should cultivate generosity, and one should train only for peace’—this is the summary of the Analysis of the Elements (Dhātuvibhaṅga).
“‘This person, bhikkhu, consists of six elements’—thus it was said.
With reference to what was this said?
There are, bhikkhu, these six elements:”
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
“This person, monk, consists of six elements”—
it is with reference to this that it was said.
‘This person, bhikkhu, consists of six bases of contact’—thus it was said.
With reference to what was this said?
The eye-base of contact, the ear-base of contact, the nose-base of contact, the tongue-base of contact, the body-base of contact, and the mind-base of contact.
‘This person, bhikkhu, consists of the six bases of contact’—
this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
‘This person, bhikkhu, consists of the eighteen mental explorations’—
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Having seen a form with the eye, one dwells upon a form that is a basis for joy, one dwells upon a form that is a basis for grief, and one dwells upon a form that is a basis for equanimity.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on].
Having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...

Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one explores a phenomenon that is a basis for joy, one explores a phenomenon that is a basis for grief, and one explores a phenomenon that is a basis for equanimity.
Thus there are six explorations of joy, six explorations of grief, and six explorations of equanimity.
“This person, bhikkhu, has eighteen explorations of the mind”—thus it was said.
Thus, that which was said— "This person, bhikkhu, has four foundations"— it was said with reference to this.
And as for what was said, "This person, bhikkhu, has four foundations," with reference to what was it said?
The foundation of wisdom, the foundation of truth, the foundation of relinquishment, and the foundation of peace.
"This person, bhikkhu, has four foundations"—
it is with reference to this that it was said.
‘One should not neglect wisdom, one should guard truth, one should cultivate generosity, and one should train only for peace’—this is what was said.
With reference to what was this said?
And how, bhikkhu, does one not neglect wisdom?
"Bhikkhus, there are these six elements:
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
And what, bhikkhus, is the earth element?"
The earth element may be internal or external.
And what, bhikkhu, is the internal earth element?
Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, hard, solid, and clung-to; that is to say:
Head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver,
midriff, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, gorge, feces, or whatever else there is internally,
belonging to oneself, that is hard, solid, and clung-to.
This, bhikkhu, is called the internal earth element.
Now, both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply the earth element.
“This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self”—thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and detaches the mind from the earth element.
And what, bhikkhu, is the water element?
The water element may be internal or it may be external.
And what, bhikkhu, is the internal water element?
Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is water or watery, and is grasped; that is to say:
bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, urine, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is water or watery, and is grasped.
This, monk, is called the internal water element.
Now, both the internal water element and the external water element are simply the water element.
“This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self”—thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the water element and detaches the mind from the water element.
And what, bhikkhu, is the fire element?
The fire element may be internal or external.
And what, monk, is the internal fire element?
Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is fire or of the nature of fire, and is clung to; that is to say:
that by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted [is digested].
Whatever internally, within oneself, is fire or fiery, clung-to, and has undergone transformation—
this, bhikkhu, is called the internal fire element. Now,
both the internal fire element and the external fire element are simply the fire element.
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus should it be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element and detaches the mind from the fire element.
And what, bhikkhu, is the air element?
The air element may be internal or external.
And what, bhikkhu, is the internal air element?
Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung-to (appropriated), such as:

Upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is air or airy,
and is clung-to— this, monks, is called the internal air element.
And as to this internal air element and the external air element, they are both simply the air element.
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus should it be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element and detaches the mind from the air element.
And what, bhikkhu, is the space element?
The space element may be internal or external.
And what, bhikkhu, is the internal space element?
That which is internal, belonging to oneself, space, spatial, and clung-to; that is to say:
The ear-cavities, the nostril-cavities, the mouth-opening, that by which one swallows what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted;
where what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted remains; and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted issues out from the lower part;
or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial in nature, void, and void in nature.
The cavity that has come to be a cavity, untouched by flesh and blood, and clung-to (upādinna)— this, bhikkhu,
is called the internal space-element.
And whatever is the internal space-element and whatever is the external space-element, that is simply the space-element.
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus should it be seen with correct wisdom as it actually is.
Having seen this with correct wisdom as it actually is, one becomes disenchanted with the space element and detaches the mind from the space element.
Then, moreover, only consciousness remains—purified and cleansed.
And what does one cognize by means of that consciousness?
One cognizes: "It is pleasant," one cognizes: "It is painful," and one cognizes: "It is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Monks, in dependence on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises.
Experiencing a pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.

One understands: "With the cessation of that very contact conducive to a pleasant feeling, that pleasant feeling which arose dependent on the contact conducive to a pleasant feeling ceases; it subsides.
Monks, dependent on a contact conducive to a painful feeling, a painful feeling arises.
Thus, when experiencing a painful feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a painful feeling.

One understands: "With the cessation of that very contact productive of pain, the corresponding experience—the painful feeling arisen in dependence on that contact productive of pain—ceases; it subsides.
Monks, in dependence on a contact productive of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
Thus, when feeling a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am feeling a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

One understands: "With the cessation of that very contact conducive to a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—which had arisen dependent on that contact conducive to a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—ceases; it subsides."
"Just as, bhikkhu, from the friction and conjunction of two pieces of wood, heat is produced and fire is generated,
yet through the separation and laying aside of those same two pieces of wood, that corresponding heat ceases and subsides; even so, bhikkhu,
dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises."
Experiencing a pleasant feeling, one understands: “I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.

One understands: “With the cessation of that very contact conducive to a pleasant feeling, the pleasant feeling arisen in dependence on that contact conducive to a pleasant feeling ceases; it subsides.
Monks, in dependence on a contact conducive to a painful feeling, a painful feeling arises.
Thus, when feeling a painful feeling, one understands: "I feel a painful feeling.
One understands: "With the cessation of that very contact productive of pain, that painful feeling which arose dependent on contact productive of pain ceases; it subsides.
Monks, dependent on contact productive of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.
Thus, when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

One understands: "With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—which arose dependent on the contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant—ceases; it subsides."
Then, furthermore, only equanimity remains— purified, bright, pliant, workable, and radiant. Just as, bhikkhu,
a skilled goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice might prepare a furnace,
and having prepared the furnace, heat the mouth of the furnace, and having heated the mouth of the furnace, take up some gold with tongs;
Suppose one were to place it in a furnace and from time to time blow upon it, from time to time sprinkle it with water,
and from time to time look on with equanimity; that gold would become well-washed,
refined, purified, and free from dross— pliant, workable, radiant— and whatever kind of ornament one might desire for it, if...
Whether it be for a headband, or earrings, or a neck-ornament, or a golden garland, he experiences that benefit;
even so, bhikkhu, what remains thereafter is equanimity alone—purified, bright, pliant, workable, and radiant.
He understands thus:
‘If I were to direct this equanimity— so pure, so bright— toward the base of infinite space and develop my mind in accordance with it,
then this equanimity of mine, supported by that and clinging to that, would endure for a very long time.
If I were to direct this equanimity— so pure, so bright— toward the base of infinite consciousness and develop my mind in accordance with it...’
In this way, this equanimity of mine, supported by that and clinging to that, would endure for a long, extended period.
If I were to direct this equanimity— so pure, so bright— toward the base of nothingness and develop my mind in accordance with it,
then this equanimity of mine, supported by that and clinging to that, would endure for a long, extended period.
‘If I were to direct this equanimity— so pure and so bright— toward the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and were to develop my mind in accordance with that state,
then this equanimity of mine, supported by that and clinging to that, would endure for a very long time. He understands thus:
‘If I were to direct this equanimity— so pure, so bright— toward the base of infinite space and develop my mind in accordance with it,
that would be conditioned.
If I were to direct this equanimity— so pure, so bright— toward the base of infinite consciousness and develop my mind in accordance with it, that would be conditioned.’
This is conditioned.
If I were to direct this equanimity— so pure, so bright— toward the base of nothingness and develop my mind in accordance with that state,
this too would be conditioned.
"If I were to direct this equanimity— so pure and so bright— toward the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and were to develop my mind in accordance with that state, thinking,
'This is conditioned,' he would neither construct nor intend it for either existence or non-existence."
Thus, not forming volitional constructions and not intending for either existence or non-existence, one does not cling to anything in the world.
Not clinging, one is not agitated; being unagitated, one personally attains final nibbāna.
One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
Thus, if he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: "It is impermanent," he understands: "It is not clung to," he understands: "It is not delighted in.
If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: "It is impermanent," he understands: "It is not clung to," he understands: "It is not delighted in.
If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: "It is impermanent," he understands: "It is not clung to," he understands: "It is not delighted in."
Thus, if he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached;
if he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached;
if he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached.

Thus, experiencing a feeling that has its limit in the body, he understands: ‘I experience a feeling that has its limit in the body. Experiencing a feeling that has its limit in life, he understands: ‘I experience a feeling that has its limit in life. He understands:
‘With the breakup of the body, after death, beyond the exhaustion of life, all that is felt here, being no longer delighted in, will become cool right here.
Just as, bhikkhu, an oil lamp burns in dependence on oil and a wick;
Just as that lamp goes out through the exhaustion of both the oil and the wick, and by not being replenished with more fuel, it is extinguished for lack of nourishment;
even so, bhikkhu, when experiencing a feeling that has the body as its limit, one understands: ‘I experience a feeling that has the body as its limit’;
when experiencing a feeling that has life as its limit, one understands: ‘I experience a feeling that has life as its limit.’
He understands: ‘I feel. He understands:
‘With the breakup of the body, after death, at the end of my life, all that is felt here, being no longer delighted in, will become cool right here.
Therefore, a bhikkhu endowed with this is possessed of this supreme foundation of wisdom.
For this, bhikkhu, is the supreme noble wisdom, namely:
the knowledge of the destruction of all suffering.
That liberation of his stands in truth and is unshakable.
For that which is deceptive, bhikkhu, is false; that which is non-deceptive, Nibbāna, is true.
Therefore, a bhikkhu endowed with this is one who possesses the supreme foundation of truth.
For this, bhikkhu, is the supreme Noble Truth, namely: [Nibbāna].
Nirvana is the state free from the nature of affliction.
Yet, previously, when he was ignorant, there were acquisitions for him that were fully undertaken and grasped.
Those have now been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future.
Therefore, a bhikkhu who is thus endowed is one who possesses this supreme foundation of generosity.
For this, bhikkhu, is the supreme noble generosity, namely:
the relinquishing of all acquisitions.
Furthermore, previously when he was ignorant, there was covetousness, desire, and lust in him;
that has now been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.
Furthermore, previously when he was ignorant, there was resentment, ill will, and malice in him.
That [craving] of his has been abandoned, its root cut off, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Furthermore, previously, when he was ignorant, there was in him ignorance and delusion;
that too has been abandoned, its root cut off, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, a bhikkhu who is thus endowed is possessed of this supreme foundation of tranquility.
For this, bhikkhu, is the supreme noble tranquility, namely:
the tranquility of lust, hatred, and delusion.
‘One should not neglect wisdom, one should guard truth, one should cultivate generosity, and one should train only for peace’—this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
‘Wherein established, the streams of conceiving do not flow; when the streams of conceiving no longer flow, one is called a sage at peace.’”
Thus indeed it was said. With reference to what was this said?
“‘I am,’ bhikkhu, this is a conceiving; ‘This I am’—this is a conceiving; ‘I shall be’—this is a conceiving; ‘I shall not be’—this is a conceiving;
‘I shall be possessed of form’—this is a conceiving; ‘I shall be formless’—this is a conceiving.”
"This is a conceiving: 'I shall be percipient'—this is a conceiving; 'I shall be non-percipient'—this is a conceiving;
'I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient'—this is a conceiving.
Conceiving, bhikkhu, is a disease; conceiving is a tumor; conceiving is a dart."
“Monk, it is precisely through the transcendence of all conceivings that one is called a sage who is at peace.
And, monk, a sage who is at peace is not born, does not age, does not die, is not disturbed, and does not crave.

For that by which he might be born does not exist for him. Being unborn, how could he age? Not aging, how could he die? Not dying, how could he be disturbed? Not being disturbed, what would he crave?”

“‘Wherein, when one stands firm, the currents of conceiving do not flow; and when the currents of conceiving do not flow, one is called a sage at peace’—it was with reference to this that this was said.
Bhikkhu, you should remember this analysis of the six elements from me in brief.”
Then the Venerable Pukkusāti, thinking, “The Teacher has indeed arrived for me;

the Sugata has indeed arrived for me; the Perfectly Enlightened One has indeed arrived for me,” rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
“A transgression, venerable sir, has overcome me—transgression born of folly, delusion, and unwholesomeness—in that I presumed to address the Blessed One with the familiar term ‘friend.’”
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression for the sake of future restraint.
“Truly, monk, you have committed a transgression—foolish, deluded, and unwholesome—as you thought it right to address me with the title ‘friend.
But since you, monk, having seen your transgression as a transgression, make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you.”

“This, bhikkhu, is growth in the discipline of the Noble One: that one who, having seen a transgression as a transgression, makes amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma, and undertakes restraint for the future.
“Venerable sir, may I receive the full ordination in the presence of the Blessed One?
“But, bhikkhu, is your bowl and robe complete?”
“Venerable sir, my bowl and robes are not yet complete.
“Bhikkhu, Tathāgatas do not grant full ordination to one whose bowl and robes are incomplete.

Then the Venerable Pukkusāti, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed to search for a bowl and robes.
Then, while the Venerable Pukkusāti was wandering about seeking a bowl and robes, a stray cow deprived him of life.

Thereupon, a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, that clansman named Pukkusāti, who had been exhorted by the Blessed One with a brief exhortation, has passed away."
“What is his destination, what is his future state?
“Bhikkhus, the clansman Pukkusāti was wise; he practiced in accordance with the Dhamma and did not trouble me regarding the Dhamma.

With the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, bhikkhus, the clansman Pukkusāti has become one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, no longer subject to return from that world.”
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, the tenth, is finished.
